instruction: As a Mitsubishi/Sodick wire-EDM controller expert, explain the following dialect detail.
input: Mitsubishi MV dialect G-codes — G29 edge-find, G30 hole-find, G54.1 work-num, G50 mirror-cancel, M103 Power Master
output: Mitsubishi MV-series WEDM dialect adds several G-codes beyond standard CNC milling. G14 sets information to variables (XYZC variable # to set Value P0). G29 is edge positioning — XY direction rapid move with R rotation angle, P edge speed, R tolerance Q (used for the auto edge-find pickup routine at job start). G30 is hole positioning — XY direction IJ rapid move (centers on a hole feature). G43.1 transfers time data into a variable (X variable # to store). G44 writes a value to a variable (P value, Q is variable). G48 is zero-point return for axes #2-4 (XYUVZ). G50 cancels mirror image (XYZC designates which axis). G54.1 sets work-number-as-work-coord (P designates work number 00-99 — used for fixturing multiple parts with offset coordinates). M103 invokes Power Master mode (Mitsubishi's proprietary adaptive-control profile), pairs with M101/M102 for state control. Post-processor authoring rule: emit M103 only when condition changes (string-select to suppress redundant emissions) — repeated M103 commands degrade performance.

instruction: Advise on the wire-EDM machining practice below.
input: JM Die E28xx taper 5-pass for 4-axis UV work — E2821-E2822-E2823-E2824-E2825
output: When cutting tapered profiles (common in extrusion die inserts and heading punches), JM Die uses the E28xx taper sequence with UV axis engagement. The E2821-E2825 family is optimized for Mitsubishi FA-20S 4-axis mode where upper and lower profiles differ. Key difference from E12xx: the E28xx roughing pass uses adaptive power compensation (M90 activated) to maintain consistent spark gap as wire angle varies. For tapers >3°, always use E28xx over E12xx. Taper capability: FA-20S supports ±15° in 3" thickness. For complex 3D profiles (different top/bottom shapes), program UV moves explicitly — do not rely on automatic taper compensation for shape differences.

instruction: As a wire-EDM CNC programming expert, explain the following programming practice.
input: H175 master offset: global trim variable for JM Die Mitsubishi FA-10S
output: JM Die uses a shop-standard H175 variable as a global master trim offset applied to ALL wire compensation H-registers. The header pattern is: 'H175 = 0.0000' followed by 'H1 = 0.0085 + H175', 'H2 = 0.0064 + H175', etc. This means the operator can adjust ALL pass offsets simultaneously by setting a single value at the machine control — for example, H175 = -0.0002 trims 0.0002 in off every pass without editing individual H values. This is critical for die work where a ±0.0001" adjustment at the machine must propagate to all 4 skim passes. Do NOT hardcode H1=0.0085 without the H175 addend — the operator has no way to trim the part at the machine. Programs without this pattern lock the operator out of fine-tuning.

instruction: Share the JM Die shop-floor wire-EDM practice for the following.
input: JM Die program-start vs per-pass-start M-code sequence are DIFFERENT — corrects ground-truth-004
output: CORRECTION + REFINEMENT of [[tip-wedm-jmd-ground-truth-004]]. The JM Die FA-10S M-code sequence is NOT a single 7-code chain. Per getJMDieMCodeSequence() in jm-die-wedm-program-patterns.ts, there are FIVE distinct phase sequences: (1) PROGRAM_START (once per program, 6 codes): M91 adaptive-OFF → M20 thread-wire → M78 fill-tank → M80 water-on → M82 wire-on → M84 power-on. (2) PER-PASS-START (once per cutting pass, 5 codes — no M91 or M20 because adaptive is toggled by M90/M91 and the wire is already threaded): M78 fill-tank → M80 water-on → M82 wire-on → M84 power-on → M90 adaptive-ON. (3) GLUE_STOP (between cutouts, 1 code): M01 optional-stop. (4) PASS_END (after rough cut to lift adaptive, 1 code): M91 adaptive-OFF. (5) PROGRAM_END (once at end, 6 codes): M85 power-off → M83 wire-off → M81 fluid-off → M21 cut-wire → M58 drain-tank → M02 program-end. So adaptive control toggles M90/M91 per-PASS (rough pass on, skim passes off — earlier tip ground-truth-004 had this right), but the OUTER program-start vs program-end frames are different M-code chains. Post-processor authoring rule: emit 5 distinct M-code blocks (program-start, per-pass-start ×N, optional glue-stops, pass-ends, program-end) — NOT one monolithic 12-code chain.

instruction: Provide wire-EDM machine maintenance guidance for the following.
input: Wire tension monitoring prevents unexpected breaks
output: Modern WEDM machines have wire tension sensors. Monitor tension variation during cutting: if tension fluctuates >15% from setpoint, the wire guides need cleaning or replacement. Contaminated guides increase friction, raising actual tension above the setpoint and causing fatigue breaks. Weekly maintenance: clean upper and lower diamond guides with a brass brush. Replace guides every 200-400 hours of cutting time depending on material abrasiveness.

instruction: Explain the wire-EDM ML / AI insight below.
input: ANN+GA optimization achieves 39.37% Ra improvement on AISI 1020
output: Hybrid Artificial Neural Network with Genetic Algorithm (ANN+GA) optimization of wire-cut EDM parameters on AISI 1020 mild steel achieves 39.37% improvement in surface roughness (Ra). Key optimized parameters: ON time, OFF time, peak current, and wire feed rate. The ANN model predicts outcomes while GA searches the parameter space for optimal combinations.

instruction: As a wire-EDM CAM expert, explain the following.
input: Mastercam Wire tab + glue-stop discipline — 1" single-contour / 2" multi-contour, M01 stop before tab cut
output: Mastercam Wire Tutorial canonical tab strategy. Single-contour parts: tab width 1.0" (1 inch). Multi-contour parts (where multiple cutouts come from one stock plate): tab width 2.0" because multiple loose parts amplify the risk of any single part dropping out at the wrong time. The tab is created by deferring the final closure of the part outline — wire cuts most of the contour, leaves a small uncut section (the tab), and finishes after the operator intervenes. A GLUE STOP (M01 optional stop) is automatically inserted before the tab-cut move when 'As glue stop' is selected for the output stop code — pauses the machine, operator secures the part with adhesive (cyanoacrylate / hot glue / clay) to prevent dropout when the tab is cut, then resumes. 'Make tab cutoff move with skim cut' is the post-discipline efficiency option — folds the tab-removal move into the final skim pass so the wire doesn't retract+re-engage for a separate cut. JM Die's M01 glue-stop frequency is 70% (per tip-wedm-jmd-ground-truth-009) — every multi-cutout production part uses this pattern.

instruction: Provide wire-EDM safety guidance for the following.
input: Used wire disposal: metal recycling, not trash
output: Used brass wire is a recyclable commodity. Collect it in the waste wire bucket (never let it overflow). Average wire consumption is 8-15 kg per 40-hour week depending on cutting volume. Current scrap brass price: $2-4/kg. More importantly: used wire in the trash can cut maintenance staff. Keep the wire collection area clean and empty the bucket daily. Some shops compact used wire into bricks for higher scrap value.

instruction: Explain the wire-EDM ML / AI insight below.
input: Multi-objective Jaya outperforms GA and TLBO for stainless steel WEDM
output: Comparative study on stainless steel wire-cut EDM optimization: Multi-objective Jaya (MO-Jaya) algorithm outperforms both Genetic Algorithm (GA) and Teaching-Learning-Based Optimization (TLBO) for simultaneously optimizing surface finish and machining time. MO-Jaya requires no algorithm-specific parameters, making it easier to implement in production settings.

instruction: You are a wire-EDM (Mitsubishi FA-series) expert. Diagnose the problem and give the corrective action.
input: Wire breaks at corners: slow feed + increase OFF time
output: Wire breaks frequently at sharp inside corners (<R0.5mm) because the wire bends around the corner while discharge energy concentrates on a smaller area. Mitigations: (1) Add corner slowdown — reduce feed to 60% at corners with radius < 2× wire diameter. (2) Increase OFF time (B) by 20-30% in corner segments. (3) Consider 0.20mm wire instead of 0.25mm for tight radii. Mitsubishi FA controllers have automatic corner control (CC) that adjusts power at corners.

instruction: You are a wire-EDM (Mitsubishi FA-series) expert. Diagnose the problem and give the corrective action.
input: Thermal distortion in thick sections: stress relief first
output: When wire-cutting thick hardened steel (>75mm), residual stresses from heat treatment cause the cut to open or close during machining. The part literally moves while you're cutting it — the wire follows a straight path but the part shifts. Mitigation: (1) stress-relieve before WEDM (sub-critical anneal at 550°C for 2h for D2/A2), (2) leave 0.5mm stock and let the part 'breathe' after rough cut, (3) re-reference before skim passes. This is the #1 cause of dimensional errors in thick WEDM work.

instruction: Advise on the wire-EDM machining practice below.
input: Mitsubishi FA-S ACU 7-pass: use only when Ra < 0.18µm (7 µin) is required
output: The Mastercam X8 Mitsubishi FA-S tech file defines an Accuracy Priority (ACU) 7-pass method for 0.010" brass wire on steel. This uses E-code families 952/5601-5607 (thin stock, 0.5") or 5611-5617 (1.00" thick). 7 passes achieves Ra 7 µin (0.18µm) — the finest surface achievable with wire EDM. However: the 7th pass adds Ra 0.025µm improvement over 6 passes at roughly 2× the skim time. Use the ACU 7-pass family only when: (a) customer specifies Ra < 8 µin (0.2µm), or (b) the feature mates with a precision-ground punch and a lapping step is not viable. For standard die work (Ra 0.4–0.8µm), stop at 5 passes — the ACU family's passes 6 and 7 are rarely cost-justified in die production.

instruction: Advise on wire-EDM quality / surface integrity for the following.
input: JM Die program quality scoring — 4 factors: completeness, correctness, optimization, safety
output: JM Die WEDM programs are scored 0-100 across 4 factors: (1) Completeness (25%): required codes present — startup sequence, E-codes, H-registers, shutdown sequence. (2) Correctness (25%): proper E-code ordering (rough before skim), offset cascade decreasing, M-code sequence valid. (3) Optimization (30%): parameters match physics benchmarks for material/thickness — feed rates, offsets, pass count appropriate. (4) Safety (20%): proper shutdown, no dangerous sequences, tank fill/drain logic correct. Programs scoring <70% should be reviewed before production. The WEDMBatchProgramAnalyzerEngine computes these scores automatically. Target score for production: >85%.

instruction: Advise on the wire-EDM machining practice below.
input: Tab with skim cuts after — efficient multi-contour slug management
output: When cutting multiple contours from a single piece of stock, use 'Tab' option with 'Make tab cutoff move with skim cut' and 'Skim cuts after tab'. This sequence: (1) Rough cuts all contours leaving tabs, (2) Skim cuts on all contours (tabs still in place), (3) Final tab burn-out cuts to release parts. Benefits: all parts remain attached during skimming for stability, batch processing is more efficient, and operator can position catch tray before tab burn-out. Set Tab Width to 1.5-2.0mm for tool steels. Add optional stop (M01 / glue stop) before tab burn-out sequence for operator intervention.

instruction: Advise on wire-EDM speeds/feeds for the situation below.
input: Skim pass count vs Ra: diminishing returns after 4 passes
output: Each skim pass improves Ra by roughly 60-70% (Toenshoff energy cascade: E_n = E_rough × 0.25^(n-1)). Typical progression: Pass 1 (rough) Ra=3.2µm → Skim 1 Ra=1.6µm → Skim 2 Ra=0.8µm → Skim 3 Ra=0.4µm → Skim 4 Ra=0.2µm. After 4 skim passes (5 total), further passes yield <0.05µm improvement — diminishing returns. For Ra<0.2µm, switch to lapping rather than adding more WEDM passes. Published data from Makino U6 confirms this plateau.

instruction: As a wire-EDM CNC programming expert, explain the following programming practice.
input: Break closest entity to thread point — creates perpendicular wire approach
output: When chaining geometry for Wire EDM, enable 'Break closest entity to thread point' in Chaining Options. This breaks the entity closest to the thread point into two pieces so the toolpath begins with a perpendicular move. Benefits: (1) creates the shortest motion between thread point and geometry, (2) ensures a clean 90° entry into the cut, (3) prevents the wire from approaching at a shallow angle that can leave witness marks. This is especially important when the thread point is outside the stock — the perpendicular approach minimizes air-cutting distance. Disable only for No Core toolpaths where the thread point IS the start point.

instruction: Explain the wire-EDM discharge physics behind the following.
input: Wire EDM spark reaches 12,000°C — material removal via local melting and evaporation
output: The spark in Wire EDM reaches temperatures up to 12,000°C, causing material removal through local melting and evaporation of the workpiece. Voltage range is typically 100V to 300V. This extreme temperature enables cutting of any conductive material regardless of hardness.

instruction: Advise on the wire-EDM machining practice below.
input: SP43/SP64 High Precision vs Both Away: choose High Precision for ±0.0001" tolerance, Both Away for form accuracy
output: The Makino SP43/SP64 MGW-S library offers two primary cutting methods for steel: High Precision and Both Away. High Precision (E-packs 1025/1035/1045/1055/1065) uses tighter servo references and lower spark energy on each pass — optimized for achieving dimensional tolerance ±0.0001" (±2.5µm) on straightforward 2D profiles with predictable deflection. Both Away (E-packs 1026/1036/1046) alternates the direction of skim passes to cancel the directional recast layer and thermal bow — preferred when the part has a tendency to bow or stress-relieve during cutting (pre-hardened tool steels above 60 HRC, asymmetric cross-sections). Both Away typically requires one additional skim pass to reach equivalent Ra, adding ~15–25% cut time. For JM Die die-making: use High Precision for standard die openings in D2/A2, Both Away for thin-web sections in S7 or pre-hardened 4140 where distortion is a concern.

instruction: Advise on the wire-EDM machining practice below.
input: JM Die M90/M91 adaptive control — enable for rough cuts, disable for final skim
output: The Mitsubishi FA-20S M90 command activates adaptive servo control (ASC), which dynamically adjusts feed rate based on spark gap stability. JM Die standard practice: M90 ON for rough cut (E1221 or E1281), first skim (E1222), and second skim (E1223). M90 OFF (M91) for final skim passes (E1224, E1225) where consistent feed rate produces better Ra. The ASC is essential for variable-thickness parts where material removal rate changes — without M90, the rough cut may undercut in thin sections or wire-break in thick sections. For uniform thickness parts, M90 is less critical but still recommended for rough and first skim.

instruction: Provide wire-EDM setup guidance for the following.
input: Taper cutting: verify UV zero offset before every job
output: Before any taper cut, verify U=0 V=0 produces a straight cut. A UV offset error of even 0.01mm translates to a taper error across the full workpiece thickness. Run a 25mm test cut in scrap material and measure top vs bottom — they should match within 0.005mm. If they don't, the UV guides need alignment. Most Mitsubishi machines have a UV alignment macro in the maintenance menu.

instruction: Advise on wire-EDM cost considerations for the following.
input: Cost-optimized mode reduces wire consumption by 40% with 15% cycle time increase
output: Counterfactual 'cost_optimized' scenario: reducing wire speed from 10→6 m/min, tension from 1200→1000g, and flush from 10→8 bar reduces wire consumption by ~40% with only 15% cycle time penalty. Recommended for production runs.

instruction: Provide wire-EDM setup guidance for the following.
input: Wire EDM work coordinate: always edge-find in X and Y
output: Set work coordinates by touching off with the wire to 2 perpendicular edges (X and Y datum surfaces). The machine's automatic edge-finding cycle energizes the wire at low power and detects first contact. Use the SAME wire for edge-finding and cutting — different wire diameters have different deflection. After edge-finding, verify by cutting a test feature and measuring. For die work, datum from the die shoe locating surfaces, not random edges.

instruction: Explain the wire-EDM ML / AI insight below.
input: Multi-pass WEDM ML framework optimizes Ra, MRR, and drum shape error
output: Generalizable machine learning framework for multi-objective optimization of multi-pass WEDM simultaneously targets: surface roughness (Ra), material removal rate (MRR), and drum shape error (DSE). Critical insight: drum shape error often overlooked in single-pass optimization becomes significant in multi-pass strategies where accumulated geometric errors compound.

instruction: Provide wire-EDM setup guidance for the following.
input: Flush nozzle alignment: 0.5mm gap to workpiece surface
output: Position the upper and lower flush nozzles 0.5mm from the workpiece surface. Too far (>2mm): flushing pressure drops, debris remains in gap, cutting speed decreases. Too close (<0.2mm): nozzle can contact workpiece during cutting, causing damage or shifting. For stepped parts where the top surface isn't flat, position the upper nozzle 0.5mm above the HIGHEST point. Some operators use shim stock as a gauge to set the gap consistently.

instruction: Advise on the wire-EDM machining practice below.
input: Makino SP43/SP64: 0.004" wire enables min inside radius of ~0.003" — use for intricate die profiles
output: The Makino SP43 and SP64 use 0.004" (0.10mm) brass wire as the standard library wire — half the diameter of the 0.008" (0.20mm) wire used on most Makino DUO and Mitsubishi FA-10S machines. This enables a minimum programmed inside corner radius of approximately 0.003" (0.076mm), compared to ~0.006" on 0.008" wire machines. Practical consequence: SP43/SP64 can cut wire guide dies, extrusion nozzles, and fine-blanking punches with inside radii that would require secondary EDM sinking or hand lapping on coarser-wire machines. Programming note: always set the lead-in to at least 2× wire diameter (0.008" min) and use straight leads, never arcs, to avoid compensation singularities at entry.

instruction: Advise on the wire-EDM machining practice below.
input: JM Die S7 shock-resistant steel — reduce power 15% to prevent micro-cracking
output: S7 shock-resistant tool steel (0.5%C, 3.25%Cr, 1.4%Mo) is used at JM Die for punches that see impact loading (cold heading, stamping). S7 at 54-58 HRC is more susceptible to thermal shock than D2/A2, leading to subsurface micro-cracks if wire EDM power is too aggressive. On the FA-20S: reduce E1221 power to 85% (vs 100% default), increase OFF time 15%, and use a 4th skim pass even for Ra 20 µin specs. Inspect first article S7 parts with dye penetrant (PT) if micro-cracking is a concern. Signs of excessive HAZ on S7: visible temper colors at cut edge, or surface roughness variation along the cut.

instruction: Advise on wire-EDM material handling for the following.
input: Diffusion-annealed gamma-phase wire — best for hardened steel + carbide + PCD
output: Brass with >40% Zn is difficult to draw, so manufacturers diffusion-anneal a heavy 18-35 µm pure-zinc coating into a CuZn37 core. The heat treatment forms gamma-phase brass at the surface (high zinc, body-centered-cubic structure), which is electrically optimal for EDM erosion. Berkenhoff MICROCUT SF is the canonical gamma-phase fine wire: CuZn37 core + gamma brass coating, tensile 1000 MPa (145,000 PSI), elongation 1%, diameter 0.05-0.10 mm with ±0.0005 mm tolerance. Recommended applications: hardened tool steel (D2/A2/M2/H13 above 60 HRC), tungsten carbide, PCD (polycrystalline diamond) cutting tools, micro-features below 200 µm. The gamma-phase wire produces a superior surface finish vs zinc-coated and dramatically better wire-break resistance vs plain brass against carbide. Never use gamma-phase wire on extreme taper jobs — 1% elongation makes it brittle for >5° taper.

instruction: Explain the wire-EDM AI optimization insight below.
input: DNN+COOT algorithm achieves 98.77% prediction accuracy for WEDM parameters
output: Combining Deep Neural Networks with Coyote Optimization Technique (COOT) algorithm achieves 98.77% accuracy in predicting optimal Wire EDM parameters. This hybrid approach handles complex non-linear relationships between process parameters.

instruction: Advise on the wire-EDM machining practice below.
input: JM Die E12xx standard 4-pass sequence for punch profiles — E1221-E1222-E1223-E1224
output: For standard punch and die profiles in tool steel (D2, A2, S7) at 0.5-2.0" thickness, JM Die uses the E12xx standard 4-pass sequence: E1221 (rough, ~0.004" overcut), E1222 (first skim, ~0.002" stock), E1223 (second skim, ~0.0015" stock), E1224 (final skim, <0.001" stock). This achieves Ra 16-20 µin reliably on the Mitsubishi FA-20S. The E1221 roughing pass runs at ~2.0 in/min on 1" D2 steel. Corresponding H-register offsets: H1=0.0085-0.010", H2=0.0064-0.0073", H3=0.0058-0.0059", H4=0.0053-0.0054". This is the workhorse sequence for 60% of JM Die production.

instruction: You are a wire-EDM (Mitsubishi FA-series) expert. Diagnose the problem and give the corrective action.
input: Flush pressure prevents wire breaks in deep cuts
output: In cuts deeper than 50mm, inadequate flushing is the #1 cause of wire breaks. Debris accumulates in the spark gap, causing short circuits and arc discharges that melt the wire. Increase flush pressure from the standard 5 bar to 8-10 bar for thicknesses >100mm. Use coaxial flushing (through the upper and lower guides) rather than side jets alone. For blind cavities where flushing is restricted, reduce cutting speed by 20-30% to compensate. Ref: Kunieda et al. CIRP 2005.

instruction: Explain the wire-EDM AI optimization insight below.
input: Ensemble ML (XGBoost + Random Forest + SVR) provides robust WEDM predictions
output: Stacking ensemble of XGBoost, Random Forest, and Support Vector Regression provides more robust predictions than individual models. The disagreement score between models indicates prediction confidence — low disagreement (<0.15) means high confidence.

instruction: Share the JM Die shop-floor wire-EDM practice for the following.
input: JM Die FA-10S E12xx 4-pass standard — rough E1221 + 3 skim E1222/E1223/E1224 (D2-class tool steel)
output: Ground truth from ITW SHAKEPROOF 500-30540-24000-04.NC production program. JM Die's standard 2-axis 4-pass straight-cut cycle on Mitsubishi FA-10S for D2 / A2 / S7 / M2 / H13 / 4140 / 4340 / O1 / W1 tool steels — uses H175 master offset. Per-pass canonical values: Pass 1 (rough) E1221 feed 0.12 ipm (3.05 mm/min) H1 offset 0.0085" (0.2159 mm). Pass 2 (skim) E1222 feed 0.24 ipm (6.10 mm/min) H2 offset 0.0064" (0.1626 mm). Pass 3 (skim) E1223 feed 0.21 ipm (5.33 mm/min) H3 offset 0.0058" (0.1473 mm). Pass 4 (skim) E1224 feed 0.20 ipm (5.08 mm/min) H4 offset 0.0053" (0.1346 mm). Offsets cascade in strictly-decreasing inches (0.0085 → 0.0064 → 0.0058 → 0.0053). Feed rate JUMPS UP between rough → skim 1 (0.12 → 0.24 — half the spark energy per unit length, so feed can double) then trends DOWN through skim 2/3 as the rim zone narrows. This is the workhorse JM Die cycle for any D2-class job that fits a 4-pass tolerance budget.

instruction: Share the JM Die shop-floor wire-EDM practice for the following.
input: JM Die E-code family selection logic — taper→E28xx, tight/thick/fine-Ra→E12xx heavy, else→E12xx standard
output: Ground truth selection logic codified in selectECodeFamily() of jm-die-wedm-tech-tables.ts, derived from JM Die shop practice. Decision tree (FIRST match wins): (1) If taper_angle > 0° AND material in [stainless, 304, 316, D2, A2, S7, M2, H13] → E28xx 5-pass UV taper. (2) If material in 2-axis families AND (tolerance < 0.005 mm OR target Ra < 0.5 µm OR thickness > 50 mm) → E12xx 5-pass HEAVY. (3) If material in 2-axis families (D2/A2/S7/M2/H13/4140/4340/O1/W1) → E12xx 4-pass STANDARD (default workhorse cycle). (4) Else (material not in JM Die's calibrated families) → return null, fall back to generic E-codes (operator must dial in conditions at the machine — JM Die does NOT have shop-calibrated cycles for materials outside their normal stock). The family-selection decision is BINDING — picking E12xx standard when the print calls Ra 0.3 µm runs the part outside JM Die's quality envelope. Wizard / AI integration rule: any wire-EDM job submitted with material+thickness+tolerance+taper+Ra should resolve to one of these 3 families OR explicitly flag 'unsupported material' — never invent a fictional E-code.

instruction: As a wire-EDM CNC programming expert, explain the following programming practice.
input: Overlap option eliminates burrs at contour start/end junction
output: The Overlap option in Mastercam Wire extends the toolpath slightly past the start point to eliminate potential burrs where the cut begins and ends. Typical overlap: 0.02mm (0.0008"). The wire cuts past the starting point, then retracts — this ensures the junction is fully cleaned. Without overlap, a small witness line or burr can remain where the first and last discharge craters meet. Use overlap on: precision die profiles, punch inserts, any feature with cosmetic requirements. Do NOT use overlap on no-core toolpaths (creates double-cut at start). The overlap motion uses skim pass power settings, not rough.

instruction: You are a wire-EDM (Mitsubishi FA-series) expert. Diagnose the problem and give the corrective action.
input: Wire breakage: reduce power before increasing tension
output: When experiencing wire breaks during roughing, reduce ON time (A/t_on) by 10-15% BEFORE increasing wire tension. High tension on a thermally weakened wire accelerates fatigue failure. Klocke (2013) shows that discharge energy is the primary wire heating mechanism — tension only matters once the wire is already near its yield point from thermal cycling. If breaks persist after ON time reduction, then increase tension by 200-300g increments.

instruction: Advise on wire-EDM machinability for the material/situation below.
input: Inconel 718 WEDM trim-pass strategy — <11 µm recast, no microhardness shift, cracking confined to recast layer
output: Inconel 718 (nickel-chromium superalloy, gas-turbine + aerospace workpiece) WEDM benchmark: with a multi-pass roughing + trimming strategy on a modern high-spec WEDM generator (designed for minimum workpiece-integrity damage), average recast layer thickness drops to <11 µm, with multiple trim passes showing 'no apparent recast or damage' in metallographic inspection. KEY FINDING: no significant change in workpiece microhardness depth-profile after WEDM (in contrast to Ti-6Al-4V, where recast hardens), and any cracking is confined to the recast layer (i.e. does NOT propagate into the base alloy). This is the operational difference between an Inconel 718 part and a Ti-6Al-4V part: Inconel tolerates higher per-spark energy without bulk-metal damage because of its higher thermal conductivity, so the parameter window is wider. Multi-response WEDM parameter optimization for Inconel 718 typically uses TGRA (Taguchi-based Grey Relational Analysis) to simultaneously optimize MRR + Ra + recast thickness. Practical setup: brass or coated brass wire, 0.25 mm dia, de-ionized water dielectric, 1 rough + 3 skim passes for tight tolerance work.

instruction: Share the JM Die shop-floor wire-EDM practice for the following.
input: JM Die parent archive — 36,928 files / 1,956 directories across 11 machine-class subtrees (WIRE EDM = 4,058 / 92 customers)
output: Parent-scope context from jm-die-archive-index.ts JM_DIE_ARCHIVE_DIRECTORIES (generated 2026-04-10): the FULL JM Die archive is 36,928 files across 1,956 directories. instruction: Provide wire-EDM setup guidance for the following.
input: Start hole positioning: 2-3mm from contour, never inside radius
output: Position the start (threading) hole 2-3mm from the contour, connected by a straight lead-in. NEVER place the start hole directly on the contour or inside a tight radius — the re-thread after wire break will fail because the hole diameter is only ~0.3mm larger than the wire, leaving no room for the wire guide to find the hole at an angle. For multiple contours, minimize start hole count by chaining contours with rapid moves between them.

instruction: You are a wire-EDM (Mitsubishi FA-series) expert. Diagnose the problem and give the corrective action.
input: D2 tool steel performance benchmark — vintage Sodick 0.010" brass: 15 in²/hr good / <5 in²/hr broken
output: Practical machinist consensus benchmark for WEDM throughput on D2 tool steel (SKD-11 in Asia), the most common WEDM workpiece material: a 1996-era Sodick with 0.010" (0.25 mm) plain brass wire should achieve 15 in²/hr (97 cm²/hr) — that's healthy throughput. 10-15 in²/hr is normal-but-aging. Below 10 in²/hr signals service is overdue (worn power-supply transistors, contaminated dielectric resin bed, fouled flush nozzles, or misaligned U-V guides). Below 5 in²/hr indicates real fault — power-supply degraded, generator dropping pulses, or wire-feed mechanism dragging. Diagnostic order: (1) check dielectric conductivity ≤5 µS/cm, (2) inspect flush pressure at both top + bottom nozzles, (3) verify wire tension at the upper guide, (4) check power-supply current draw against spec, (5) confirm filter / resin bed not loaded. Zn-coated wire shifts these benchmarks up by 20-30%.

instruction: Advise on the wire-EDM machining practice below.
input: JM Die E12xx heavy 5-pass for thick stock and cannelure dies — E1281-E1282-E1283-E1284-E1285
output: For thicker tool steel (>2" up to 6") and cannelure (thread roll) dies that require superior surface finish, JM Die uses the E12xx heavy 5-pass sequence: E1281-E1285. The E128x family has higher power settings than E122x for roughing but adds a 5th skim pass for better Ra. Typical application: FIOCCHI 38 CAL CANNELURE 30TPI dies requiring <12 µin Ra on the thread profile. The 5th pass adds 8-12 minutes per profile but eliminates manual polishing. Use E128x when: (1) thickness >2.5", (2) Ra requirement <16 µin, (3) customer specified no secondary finishing, or (4) complex profiles where manual polish is difficult.

instruction: Provide wire-EDM setup guidance for the following.
input: JM Die Mitsubishi FA startup sequence — M78-M80-M82-M84 then M20
output: JM Die programs follow the standard Mitsubishi FA startup M-code sequence: M78 (fill tank), M80 (water circulation on), M82 (wire drive on), M84 (power supply on), then M20 (thread wire through start hole). After M20, move to first approach point (G0), then engage M90 (adaptive control) before the first cut (G1). Do NOT skip M78 — even though the tank may already be full from the previous job, M78 confirms fill level and opens the correct valves. Skipping M78 on the FA-20S can cause improper flushing nozzle engagement.

instruction: As a wire-EDM CNC programming expert, explain the following programming practice.
input: TECH library contains machine-specific power sequences up to 24 passes
output: Mastercam Wire uses TECH libraries (.TECH files) that contain manufacturer-calibrated power settings, feed rates, wire offsets, and register values for specific wire EDM machines. A TECH library can define up to 24 passes for a single material/thickness combination. Example sequences: Rough & 2 Skim(s), Rough & 3 Skim(s), Rough & 4 Skim(s). When loading a TECH library, Mastercam populates all electrical parameters (A, B, C registers), feed rates, and compensation values. Manufacturer-provided TECH libraries (Mitsubishi, Makino, Fanuc) are optimized for that machine's power supply. Always use TECH libraries for production — never manually enter power settings unless you're a Wire EDM specialist.

instruction: Share the wire-EDM tactic for the following situation.
input: Wire-break risk axes — thickness × material × corner-radius × flushing (wizard validation gate)
output: Canonical wire-break risk-axes checklist from existing tribal tip [[tip-jm-die-019]] (conf 91). Four independent axes that compound multiplicatively — a job that's tall AND hard AND tight-cornered AND poorly-flushed has Π(risk_i) probability of breaking, not Σ. (1) THICKNESS — taller workpiece = longer wire span = more thermal accumulation per spark + more deflection under flushing pressure. Above 100 mm switch to hard-brass or coated wire ([[tip-wedm-wiki-tactic-002]]). (2) MATERIAL — high-conductivity / high-melting-point workpieces (carbide / Inconel / hardened steel) draw more current per spark + heat the wire faster than low-conductivity stock. (3) CORNER RADIUS — tight internal radii force the wire to dwell at the corner while it traverses the geometric singularity; dwell + high discharge = breaks. Below 0.10 mm internal radius is in the danger zone for 0.25 mm brass wire (min radius ≈ wire_radius + spark_gap). (4) FLUSHING — bad flushing → debris accumulates → arc instability → DC arcing (the most damaging mode for wire integrity, far worse than steady erosion). Wizard validation gate rule: if 3-of-4 axes flag risk, REQUIRE operator confirmation before generating the program; if 4-of-4, DOWNGRADE pass-count target or RAISE wire-tier (coated → hard-brass-coated → gamma-phase). Mirrors fail-loud R12 — surfaces high-risk jobs before they break in production.

instruction: Advise on wire-EDM quality / surface integrity for the following.
input: JM Die offset cascade verification — H-values must strictly decrease per pass
output: A critical quality check for any JM Die wire EDM program: H-register offset values must strictly decrease from rough to final skim. Typical cascade: H1=0.0085 > H2=0.0068 > H3=0.0059 > H4=0.0054 (inches). If any H-value equals or exceeds the previous pass, the wire will re-cut the same material or leave stock — both cause quality issues. The neural analysis engine flags 'AP003: Offset increases between passes' as a major anti-pattern. When reviewing programs, verify: H[n+1] < H[n] for all passes. The decrement between passes should be 0.0005-0.0015" — smaller decrements are fine for precision, but larger decrements indicate missing passes.

instruction: As a Mitsubishi/Sodick wire-EDM controller expert, explain the following dialect detail.
input: Sodick IP-parameter cap is generator-tier-locked — NF25=15, NF40=31.5, NF80=63.5
output: On Sodick AQ/NF-series controllers, peak current IP is set as a discrete integer 0-15 (or 0-63 on later generators) that selects the number of Tr (transistor) circuits switched in parallel. The maximum IP available is locked to the machine's generator class: NF25 generator caps at IP=15.15 max, NF40 caps at 31.5, NF80 caps at 63.5. Setting IP above the generator cap is silently floored — the operator sees 'IP=63' on the screen, but the generator only switches 31 transistors. This is the #1 cause of 'why is my new cutting condition slower than the old one' confusion when condition files are imported from a higher-tier machine. The mean machining current IA shown on the ammeter equals IP × (TON / (TON + TOFF + standby)), so a higher IP cap directly raises achievable MRR for the same TON/TOFF — generator class is the dominant performance lever, not condition-file tweaking. Source: DMNC EDM 'Discharging Conditions, Parameters Explanation of CNC EDM Machine' PDF.

instruction: Provide wire-EDM setup guidance for the following.
input: JM Die glue stop convention — M01 before tab burn-out points
output: JM Die uses M01 (optional stop) at strategic points in wire EDM programs for operator intervention, typically: (1) before burning out glue tabs (allows operator to reduce tank level and position catch tray), (2) at major slug drop points where manual extraction is needed, (3) before final skim on critical tolerance features. The M01 is optional stop, not M00 mandatory stop — this allows unattended runs when the operator cycles 'optional stop OFF' on the controller. During setup runs, keep optional stop ON; for production runs, turn it OFF for continuous cutting.

instruction: Advise on the wire-EDM machining practice below.
input: JM Die tungsten carbide — zinc-coated wire mandatory, E952+E56xx ACU sequence
output: Tungsten carbide (WC-Co, 6-15% cobalt) is used at JM Die for wear-critical die inserts and forming tools. Wire EDM of WC on the FA-20S requires: (1) zinc-coated brass wire (not plain brass) — the zinc coating prevents wire breakage in the high-energy rough cut, (2) E952 ACU roughing followed by E56xx ACU skim sequence (E5621-E5622-E5623 or E5627), (3) reduced flushing pressure (4 bar vs 6 bar for steel) to prevent wire deflection in the harder kerf. Cutting rate is 40-50% of steel due to WC's low electrical conductivity. Always run 4+ skim passes on WC — the cobalt binder melts preferentially during EDM, creating a cobalt-depleted surface layer that must be removed.

instruction: As a wire-EDM CAM expert, explain the following.
input: Mastercam Wire 'Break closest entity to thread point' — chaining option critical for AWT-reliable thread-point geometry
output: Mastercam Wire Tutorial chaining option 'Break closest entity to thread point' (default-ON in the tutorial) — splits the contour geometry at the operator-selected thread-point location so the wire enters cleanly from the start-hole into the cutting path. WITHOUT this option: the wire enters the contour at the nearest geometric entity vertex (which may be tens of mm away from the start-hole), forcing the wire to traverse uncut material to reach the contour — increases threading time + raises break risk during the traverse. WITH this option: a geometry-break-point is inserted at the thread point so the wire enters the contour AT the start hole. Multi-contour 'Window chaining' (drag-rectangle to select multiple parts simultaneously) PRESERVES this option per-contour. Wizard / AI rule: this option must be explicitly preserved in any Mastercam-derived program; ignoring it produces nominally-correct G-code that AWT (auto wire threader) cannot reliably thread to on the FA-10S because the thread-point and the geometry-entry-point are mismatched.

instruction: As a Mitsubishi/Sodick wire-EDM controller expert, explain the following dialect detail.
input: Makino Hyper-i M-code program skeleton — M06 thread → M17 start → G01 + G42 cut → M18 stop → M07 cut → M30
output: Canonical Makino WEDM program (U6 H.E.A.T., U86, UX6 — Hyper-i control) follows a 6-step M-code skeleton. Header: G90 G54 G00 X0 Y0, G00 Z0 (positioning), TECH-NNNN/9002 (tech table call), E21 D21 register pair (E21 = tech, D21 = offset). Then the body sequence: M06 (auto-thread wire), M17 (start machining — turns ON water + wire + electricity simultaneously), G01 G42 (linear move with right-side compensation) + XY axis moves to traverse the cut, M18 (stop machining — turns OFF water + wire + electricity), M07 (cut wire — at the end of part or at a glue stop), M30 (end of program). Taper programs (UV-axis) layer onto this without changing the M-code skeleton. K-generator is the older Makino generator family (nanosecond pulse delivery), HFG (High Frequency Generator) is the newer family (higher frequency at lower current for better surface finish). U86 published throughput: cycle time -50% vs prior generation, surface finish 3 µm Rmax in 3 passes (1 rough + 2 skim), machining speed up to 350 mm²/min, positioning accuracy ±1 µm, repeatability 2 µm.

instruction: Advise on wire-EDM wire / consumable selection for the following.
input: Coated wire reduces breaks in carbide and PCD
output: When cutting tungsten carbide (WC) or PCD (polycrystalline diamond), use zinc-coated brass wire instead of plain brass. The zinc coating acts as a sacrificial layer, vaporizing during discharge and improving flushing. Typical improvement: 30-50% fewer wire breaks at equivalent cutting speed. Zinc-coated wire costs ~40% more but saves 2-3 hours per job in reduced downtime from breaks. For WC thicker than 30mm, gamma-phase coated wire (e.g., Bedra Megacut Plus) is recommended.

instruction: Share the JM Die shop-floor wire-EDM practice for the following.
input: JM Die FA-10S E12xx 5-pass heavy — rough E1281 + 4 skim E1282-E1285 (cannelure / thick / tight-tol)
output: Ground truth from CHOCTAW DEFENSE 38 CAL CANNELURE and FIOCCHI 38 CAL CANNELURE production programs. JM Die's heavy-duty 2-axis 5-pass cycle on Mitsubishi FA-10S — auto-selected when tolerance < 0.005 mm OR target Ra < 0.5 µm OR thickness > 50 mm. Applies to D2 / A2 / S7 / M2 / H13. Per-pass canonical values: Pass 1 (rough) E1281 feed 0.06 ipm (1.52 mm/min) H1 offset 0.00995" (0.2527 mm) — SLOWER than 4-pass rough because heavier rim zone burned for finer subsequent passes. Pass 2 (skim) E1282 feed 0.15 ipm (3.81 mm/min) H2 offset 0.00725" (0.1842 mm). Pass 3 (skim) E1283 feed 0.12 ipm (3.05 mm/min) H3 offset 0.00585" (0.1486 mm). Pass 4 (skim) E1284 feed 0.16 ipm (4.06 mm/min) H4 offset 0.00535" (0.1359 mm). Pass 5 (skim) E1285 feed 0.13 ipm (3.30 mm/min) H5 offset 0.0052" (0.1321 mm). Distinguishing characteristic vs the 4-pass: starting offset is HIGHER (0.00995 vs 0.0085) and there's an extra finishing pass squeezing the rim zone smaller. Reach-for-it cycle when the print calls a class-2 ground-die-equivalent surface finish or extreme tolerance.

instruction: Advise on wire-EDM speeds/feeds for the situation below.
input: Skim pass feed rate does NOT monotonically decrease — peak at pass 3
output: Common intuition says each successive WEDM skim pass should be slower (finer cut = slower). JM Die's actual production programs contradict this. In the E28xx taper 5-pass family (NOZE TEST.NC): Pass1=F0.16, Pass2=F0.23, Pass3=F0.26, Pass4=F0.30, Pass5=no feed specified. In the E12xx standard 4-pass family: Pass1=F0.12, Pass2=F0.24, Pass3=F0.21, Pass4=F0.20. The pattern is clear: Pass 2 is significantly faster than Pass 1, Pass 3 is sometimes faster than Pass 2, and final passes slow slightly. Explanation: Pass 1 (rough) is feed-rate limited by debris clearing; Pass 2 removes the bulk of recast and runs fast because discharge craters are still relatively large; later passes slow as crater size shrinks and spark energy must be reduced. Never slow all skim passes uniformly — use the E-code family's calibrated feed sequence.

instruction: Provide wire-EDM setup guidance for the following.
input: JM Die H175 master offset convention — use H175 as the primary offset base
output: JM Die programs consistently use H175 as the master offset register for rough cut geometry. When setting up a new program, declare H175 first with the total wire + overburn offset (typically 0.0085-0.010"), then cascade H1-H4 or H1-H5 for skim passes with decreasing values. The H175 convention allows quick offset adjustments at the machine without editing the program — the operator can tweak H175 by ±0.0005" to dial in the first part. This is a JM Die shop standard that differs from the Mastercam default of H1 as primary. When training AI on JM Die programs, recognize H175 as the master offset, not H1.

instruction: As a Mitsubishi/Sodick wire-EDM controller expert, explain the following dialect detail.
input: Mitsubishi MV1200/MV2400 auto-E-pack (AD program) vs older FX10 manual offset selection
output: Major dialect break between Mitsubishi FX-series and newer MV-series WEDM controllers. On older FX10, the operator picks an E-pack number from a printed technology book (rows = wire diameter × thickness × material; columns = roughing vs skim passes), then keys in the matching kerf offset manually. On MV1200S / MV2400-ST Advance Type M800 with M800-series control, there is NO E-pack number to enter and NO offset value to key — the operator selects material type + workpiece thickness + wire diameter, and the AD program (auto-E-pack-from-material) resolves the full E-pack + offset automatically. This is the #1 dialect-confusion when porting a CAM post from an FX10 site to an MV1200 site: the FX10 post emits the E-pack number + offset register in the program header; the MV1200 ignores them in favor of its AD selection, and the operator sees 'wrong condition' if the post doesn't switch to AD-mode header. Generator-tier-dependent: same E-pack number on FX10 vs MV1200 cuts at different rates because their generator's power envelope differs.

instruction: Share the JM Die shop-floor wire-EDM practice for the following.
input: JM Die FA-10S E28xx 5-pass UV taper — stainless die work, zero H-offset convention (taper geometry encodes kerf)
output: Ground truth from NOZE TEST.NC production program. JM Die's 4-axis UV taper 5-pass cycle on Mitsubishi FA-10S — applies to stainless 304 / 316 / 17-4 PH AND D2 / A2 / S7 / M2 / H13 when the print specifies a taper angle > 0°. Per-pass canonical values: Pass 1 (rough) E2821 feed 0.16 ipm (4.06 mm/min). Pass 2 (skim) E2822 feed 0.23 ipm (5.84 mm/min). Pass 3 (skim) E2823 feed 0.26 ipm (6.60 mm/min). Pass 4 (skim) E2824 feed 0.30 ipm (7.62 mm/min). Pass 5 (skim) E2825 feed operator-entered at machine. KEY CONVENTION: all H-register offsets are ZERO (H1=H2=H3=H4=H5=0.0000) on taper programs — UNLIKE the 2-axis E12xx family. Taper compensation is encoded in the U-V geometry path itself, NOT in kerf-offset registers. This means H175 master-offset trim does NOT apply to E28xx cycles. Operator dials in size by editing the UV taper angle or geometry, NOT by adjusting H-values. Common gotcha: AI / CAM systems that auto-apply H175 trim to E28xx cycles distort the taper geometry. Feed rate trend on taper is the OPPOSITE of E12xx — accelerates monotonically (0.16 → 0.23 → 0.26 → 0.30) because each skim removes less metal at narrower rim zones AND the UV mechanism damps wire bow on a tapered cut.

instruction: Explain the wire-EDM discharge physics behind the following.
input: Longer pulse-on time reduces MRR due to ion energy sharing — shorter pulses more efficient

instruction: You are a wire-EDM (Mitsubishi FA-series) expert. Diagnose the problem and give the corrective action.
input: JM Die wire break risk factors — thickness, material, corner radius, flushing
output: JM Die's wire break risk model (0-100 scale) considers 4 primary factors: (1) Thickness: <25mm=low, 25-75mm=medium, >75mm=high risk — add 15 points per category. (2) Material: tool steel=base, stainless=+10, carbide=+25. (3) Corner radius: >2mm=0, 1-2mm=+10, 0.5-1mm=+20, <0.5mm=+30. (4) Flushing: open=0, semi-closed=+10, fully enclosed (blind cavity)=+25. instruction: You are a wire-EDM (Mitsubishi FA-series) expert. Diagnose the problem and give the corrective action.
input: Ra worse than expected: check water resistivity first
output: If surface finish (Ra) is 20-50% worse than predicted, check the dielectric water resistivity FIRST. Optimal range for finishing: 5-15 MΩ·cm (deionized). Resistivity below 3 MΩ·cm causes unstable discharges with irregular crater sizes → worse Ra. The deionizing resin needs replacement when resistivity drops below 3 MΩ·cm under load. Most machines have a resistivity gauge on the tank — check it before adjusting E-pack parameters.

instruction: You are a wire-EDM (Mitsubishi FA-series) expert. Diagnose the problem and give the corrective action.
input: Makino SP43/SP64 vs Mitsubishi FA-10S: E-pack numbering is incompatible — never cross-apply codes
output: Makino MGW-S E-packs (SP43/SP64) use a completely different numbering and power parameter scheme from Mitsubishi FA-10S E-codes. Makino steel High Precision uses 1XXX roughing (e.g., 1025, 1035, 1045) + 12XX skim passes. Mitsubishi steel uses E12XX series (E1221–E1285). Despite the superficial similarity, these codes are NOT interchangeable — voltage, pulse width, servo reference, and flushing parameters all differ. Loading Makino codes on a Mitsubishi (or vice versa) will at minimum produce wrong surface finish, and at worst cause wire breaks and part damage. Mitsubishi carbide uses E-codes in the 5XXX range; Makino carbide ALSO uses 5XXX range (5025, 5035...) — this overlap makes the confusion especially dangerous. Always verify the machine type and control before selecting an E-pack family.

instruction: Advise on the wire-EDM machining practice below.
input: Both Away Precision beats High Speed for die work: 2~2.5µm Ra in 5 passes on Makino DUO
output: Makino DUO tech tables define six cutting methods per wire/material combo. For die and tooling work requiring Ra < 3µm: always choose Both Away Precision. This method approaches the final dimension from both sides (rough cut leaves +offset, each skim cuts from the outside in alternating directions), eliminating the directional recast bias of single-direction methods. Measured results from Mastercam X8 DUO-Ver6-METRIC tech file: 0.20mm BS wire, steel, 10mm thick — Both Away Precision achieves Ra 2~2.5µm in 5 passes (rough 1036 + 4 skims E1535–E1538). The final offset is 0.107mm (approximately wire radius + 0.007mm spark gap). High Speed method achieves only Ra 18~20µm in 1 pass and is unsuitable for precision die work.

instruction: Provide wire-EDM safety guidance for the following.
input: Fire risk: maintain water level above workpiece
output: Wire EDM dielectric fluid (deionized water) must ALWAYS cover the workpiece during cutting. Exposed sparking above the waterline can ignite dielectric additives, workpiece oil residue, or create explosive hydrogen gas pockets. Monitor the tank level sensor — if the level drops below the workpiece top (pump failure, leak, evaporation), the machine should auto-pause. For submerged mode, maintain at least 25mm water coverage above the top of the workpiece.

instruction: Advise on wire-EDM machinability for the material/situation below.
input: Ti-6Al-4V WEDM recast layer 10-70 µm sinker / <11 µm optimized trim passes — fatigue loss 15-30%
output:
Titanium Ti-6Al-4V (TC4) is the most-studied difficult-to-machine WEDM workpiece due to aerospace + medical demand. Recast-layer thickness range: 10-70 µm on single-pass sinker EDM, dropping to <11 µm with optimized WEDM multi-pass strategy (1 rough + 2-3 skim trim passes). Recast layer causes microhardness elevation from 132 HV (base material) to 161-338 HV (recast surface) — the recast is HARDER than the base but contains micro-cracks. Fatigue strength reduction 15-30% due to combined recast + increased surface roughness (cracks initiate at the recast/base interface). Reduction strategy: lower peak current Ip + use multi-pass + de-ionized water dielectric (NOT oil — oil generates carbon-laden recast on Ti). Brass wire is the standard electrode for Ti; coated wire shifts crater geometry to extended-and-shallow (better for Ra) at the cost of MRR. Best generator combo for Ti finishing: short TON (3-6 µs), long TOFF (60-100 µs), low Ip (1-3 A), high servo voltage (50-80 V) — this minimizes the per-spark energy and keeps recast thin. Cracks can completely disappear by decreasing peak current in LS-WEDT (low-speed wire-EDM-turning), differing from standard LS-WEDM behavior.

Shop-calibrated reference: Bedra Berkenhoff BEDRA TOPAS PLUS zinc_coated_brass, diameter 0.25 mm, operating tension 14 N.

input: DC vs AC power supply affects Ra on aluminum

instruction: Share the JM Die shop-floor wire-EDM practice for the following.
input: JM Die customer part-number regex patterns — auto-detect customer from PN at quote-intake
output: Per-customer part-number regex patterns from jm-die-archive-index.ts JM_DIE_CUSTOMERS_INDEXED — usable by the wire-wizard's intake form to auto-detect customer from a pasted PN. instruction: As a wire-EDM CNC programming expert, explain the following programming practice.
input: Maximum leadout shortens travel from contour end to cut point
output: The Maximum Leadout option in Mastercam Wire shortens the lead-out move instead of forcing the wire to travel the full distance from contour end to cut point. Set a maximum distance (e.g., 0.3mm) — the lead-out will be truncated if it would exceed this length. Use when: (1) thread point is far from contour geometry, (2) multiple contours share a common thread point region, (3) minimizing air-cutting time is critical. Do NOT use maximum leadout on critical tolerance features where full lead-out is needed for dimensional accuracy. The shortened lead-out can cause slight dimensional variation at the cut completion point.

instruction: Advise on wire-EDM process parameters for the situation below.
input: Zinc-coated optimal MRR parameter combo — 30 m/min, TON 120 / TOFF 50 µs, IP 2 A, V 20
output: Taguchi DOE study on Zn-Coated Brass wire found an optimal-MRR parameter combo: wire feed 30 m/min, pulse-on TON 120 µs, pulse-off TOFF 50 µs, peak current IP 2 A, servo voltage V 20 V. Material removal rate (MRR) and surface roughness scale UP with TON and IP; both scale DOWN with TOFF and servo voltage. The MRR-optimal combo trades surface roughness — for kerf-width-optimal on Half-Hard wire the combo shifts to wire feed 8 m/min, TON 110 µs, TOFF 60 µs (slower feed + slightly longer TOFF stabilize the gap and tighten the kerf). On vintage Sodick at 0.010" plain brass cutting D2 tool steel (SKD-11 in Asia), 15 in²/hr is healthy throughput, below 10 in²/hr suggests need for maintenance, below 5 in²/hr indicates a real fault. Use these as parameter-tuning anchors, not absolute values — your machine generator + wire + dielectric conductivity will shift the optimum.

instruction: As a wire-EDM CNC programming expert, explain the following programming practice.
input: Always use double M78 M78 for tank fill on Mitsubishi FA-10S
output: On the Mitsubishi FA-10S at JM Die, the Fill Tank command M78 is ALWAYS issued twice in succession (M78 M78) before every cut restart. This is not a typo — a single M78 starts the pump but the FA-10S requires a second M78 to confirm and hold the fill state during re-threading. The double command appears in every production program analyzed (ITW SHAKEPROOF, NOZE TEST, CHOCTAW DEFENSE cannelure) — 100% consistency. Writing only a single M78 causes intermittent 'insufficient fluid' alarms during AWT (Automatic Wire Threading) because the machine checks tank level mid-thread. Always write 'M78 M78' as a unit.

instruction: Advise on wire-EDM speeds/feeds for the situation below.
input: Reduce flush pressure during skim passes
output: High flush pressure (8-10 bar) is needed for roughing to clear heavy debris. But during skim passes, REDUCE flush to 3-5 bar. High pressure on skim passes causes wire vibration, degrading surface finish. The debris load during skimming is minimal (tiny craters), so aggressive flushing is unnecessary. Some machines have automatic flush pressure scheduling per pass — enable it in the E-pack technology table. This alone can improve skim Ra by 10-15%.

instruction: Provide wire-EDM setup guidance for the following.
input: Submerged vs non-submerged: always submerge when possible
output: Submerged wire cutting (tank filled above workpiece) improves cutting speed by 10-15% and reduces wire breaks by 20-30% compared to spray/jet flushing. The dielectric bath provides uniform cooling and consistent flushing from all directions. The ONLY reasons to cut non-submerged: (1) workpiece too tall for the tank, (2) real-time visual inspection needed, (3) magnetically clamped parts (water pressure can shift them). For production, submerged cutting is the default.

instruction: Explain the wire-EDM dielectric/chemistry consideration below.
input: WEDM dielectric water — keep κw ~1 µS/cm via mixed-bed resin; aluminum spikes conductivity fast
output: WEDM dielectric is deionized water held at conductivity κw ~1 µS/cm by continuous filtration through a mixed-bed ion-exchange resin (cation + anion beads in one tank). The dielectric stack: workpiece tank → coarse magnetic separator (catches steel chips) → 3-5 µm paper-cartridge filter (catches fine debris) → mixed-bed resin tank (removes metal ions) → conductivity sensor → recirculate. Tap water is acceptable for first fill IF passed through DI resin once; pre-distilled or RO water is preferred — making the DI system 'maintain' clean water is far cheaper than making it 'recover' fouled water. Cutting ALUMINUM raises κw 5-10x faster than cutting steel — Al ions saturate the resin in hours, not weeks. When the conductivity sensor alarms (typically at 10-20 µS/cm), the resin tank must be regenerated (factory cycle) or replaced; running fouled dielectric causes wire breaks, missed sparks (ignition-delay collapses), and visible surface degradation. Filter cartridges replace on a debris-not-time schedule — Δpressure across the filter is the trigger. High-speed cutting at 300 PSI flush triples-to-quadruples the pump+filter+resin load — plan resin regeneration cycles 3-4x more frequent.

instruction: As a wire-EDM CAM expert, explain the following.
input: Mastercam Wire 4-pass canonical overburn cascade — 0.035 → 0.02 → 0.01 → 0 on Ø0.2 mm wire

Tutorial verbatim: 'As the passes get closer to the final part shape, the wire cuts less material and the overburn decreases.' Default Additional Skim Cuts (before tab) = 3 in the tutorial example — i.e. rough + 3 skim = 4 passes. The wire diameter parameter is explicitly entered per-pass starting at pass 2 (operator may vary wire between rough and skim — but in the tutorial it stays 0.2 across all skims). This 4-pass / Ø0.2 mm / 0.035→0 cascade is what every Mastercam Wire post emits by default, and what JM Die's E12xx 4-pass family matches at the Mitsubishi E-pack level (E1221-E1224). Wizard / AI rule: when a user submits with no parameter overrides, present this Mastercam-canonical default as the safe starting point — operator can override per-job.

instruction: Share the JM Die shop-floor wire-EDM practice for the following.

instruction: You are a wire-EDM (Mitsubishi FA-series) expert. Diagnose the problem and give the corrective action.
input: Wire break recovery: re-thread 2mm behind break point
output: After a wire break, re-thread the wire 2-3mm behind the break point and restart. Do NOT restart from the exact break location — debris and recast layer at the break point cause immediate re-break. Most Mitsubishi and Sodick machines have automatic wire re-threading (AWT) but set the backup distance in the controller parameters. For production: set auto-retry count to 3 with 2mm backup. If it breaks 3 times at the same location, the machine should alarm and notify the operator.

instruction: Advise on the wire-EDM machining practice below.
input: JM Die H13 hot work steel — reduce power 20% for large dies to prevent cracking
output: H13 hot work tool steel (0.4%C, 5%Cr, 1.3%Mo, 1%V) at 44-52 HRC is used at JM Die for hot heading dies and aluminum extrusion tooling. H13's lower carbon content and lower hardness make it more sensitive to thermal shock than the cold work steels. For wire EDM on FA-20S: reduce E1221 power to 80%, increase OFF time 20%, and consider using the E952 ACU (Adaptive Control Unit) mode for large cavities. H13 is also prone to delayed cracking — inspect parts 24-48 hours after wire EDM, not immediately. For H13 thicker than 3", consider stress relief (1050°F for 2 hours) before wire EDM.

instruction: Advise on the wire-EDM machining practice below.
input: Cannelure/thread WEDM: alternate G2/G3 arcs with G1 flanks for thread form
output: JM Die uses Wire EDM to cut cannelure grooves and thread profiles in hardened die steels — a specialty technique for ammo/fastener tooling (Choctaw Defense, Fiocchi). The pattern: the thread form is approximated as alternating short G2 (CW arc) and G3 (CCW arc) segments for the thread radius, with G1 linear segments for the thread flanks. For a 30 TPI cannelure at ~0.0333" pitch: G1 flank approach → G2 X... I-.00206 J.00218 (CW arc, ~0.003" radius) → G1 X... (next flank) → G3 X... I0. J.003 (CCW arc back) → repeat. The pass 1 uses G2 for one arc direction, pass 2 reverses to G3 — this alternation prevents residual material on one flank. Key insight: the arc radius (~0.003") is sized to the wire diameter (0.010") plus desired root radius. For defense/aerospace customers this technique eliminates hand-finishing of thread roots.

instruction: Advise on wire-EDM machinability for the material/situation below.
input: Tungsten carbide WC-Co WEDM — cobalt binder erodes first, 2000-3000 mm²/hr MRR, recast scales with duty factor
output: Tungsten carbide WC-Co (cobalt binder typically 6-15 wt%) is the second most-common WEDM workpiece after tool steel — used for stamping dies, punches, milling-insert seats, and wear plates. The cobalt binder erodes PREFERENTIALLY to tungsten because Co has superior electrical conductivity to WC — the WEDM process selectively dislodges WC grains by melting their cobalt matrix, creating the characteristic 'WC-dislodgement craters' visible under SEM. Practical MRR is 2000-3000 mm²/hr — about 30% of tool-steel MRR. Recast layer thickness + micro-crack length both scale UP with peak current + duty factor (TON / (TON+TOFF)). Strategy: use main-cut + multiple trim-cut passes with declining IP per pass; modern generators achieve <0.3 µm rim-zone (recast + white-layer) on the final skim. CH-based (hydrocarbon) sinker EDM produces LOWER tensile residual stress than water-based WEDM — but WEDM kerf geometry usually mandates water. Stress-relief annealing at 500°C × 2 hr in vacuum reduces residual stress ≥70% before/after WEDM. INSPECTION DISCIPLINE: SEM-scan every WC-Co WEDM part for surface cracks before downstream processing; recast cracks can propagate under stamping load.

instruction: Provide wire-EDM setup guidance for the following.
input: SP43/SP64 flushing: upper and lower nozzle standoff is critical — maintain ≤ 0.010" gap
output: The Makino SP43/SP64 with 0.004" wire uses very small upper and lower flushing nozzles. The nozzle standoff (distance from nozzle face to workpiece surface) must be ≤ 0.010" (0.25mm) to maintain adequate coaxial flush pressure around the 0.004" wire. With the MGW-S control, flushing pressure is set automatically by the E-pack condition — the operator only needs to verify nozzle position. Symptoms of excessive standoff: wire breaks in the middle of long straight cuts (not at corners), inconsistent Ra from top to bottom of the cut, and visible debris accumulation in the cut kerf. For interrupted surfaces (holes, slots, or stepped workpieces), use the machine's broken-surface flushing mode — on MGW-S this is activated via the C-cycle parameter. Do NOT use standard nozzle-flush on workpieces with openings larger than 0.5" in the flushing path — use submerged (immersion) cutting instead.

instruction: Advise on the wire-EDM machining practice below.
input: Maximum practical WEDM thickness depends on wire type
output: Maximum recommended cutting thickness by wire type: 0.20mm brass wire = 100mm, 0.25mm brass wire = 200mm, 0.30mm brass wire = 300mm, 0.25mm coated wire = 250mm. Beyond these limits, wire deflection under discharge force exceeds acceptable tolerance (δ = F×L²/8T where L=thickness). For thicknesses >200mm, consider sinker EDM instead. Practical limit for production: 150mm with 0.25mm wire for repeatability.

instruction: Explain the wire-EDM dielectric/chemistry consideration below.
input: WEDM flushing nozzles — top + bottom 'rooster tail' rule; too-high pressure deflects wire on tall workpieces
output: WEDM uses TWO opposing flush nozzles — one above the workpiece (top guide) and one below (lower guide) — to push dielectric into the cutting gap from both sides simultaneously. When properly tuned, the two streams meet in the middle of the workpiece thickness and produce the visible 'rooster tail' effect — a turbulent plume at the kerf exit. The rooster tail indicates flushing is balanced; if only one nozzle's stream is visible, the other is plugged or its pressure is set too low (rebalance before cutting more — uneven flush causes asymmetric thermal load and tapered kerf). Pressure rule: 2-8 bar for thin parts (<25 mm), 8-15 bar for thick parts (>50 mm), and up to 20 bar (300 PSI) for high-speed roughing on very thick / very dense materials. BUT too-high flush pressure on a TALL workpiece deflects the wire visibly — wire bow can exceed 50 µm on a 200 mm-thick part with 15 bar flush, ruining straightness tolerance. Diagnostic: if surface finish is striated parallel to cut direction (vertical lines on the side wall), wire is bowing — drop flush pressure 20%. Practical Sodick/Mitsubishi setting: begin with 5 bar both nozzles, raise upper or lower until rooster tail symmetrizes.

instruction: Advise on wire-EDM speeds/feeds for the situation below.
input: Thick section (>50mm): flushing efficiency degrades as 1/sqrt(thickness)
output: For sections thicker than 50mm, flushing efficiency degrades approximately as 1/sqrt(thickness/50). At 100mm thickness, flushing is ~71% efficient; at 150mm, ~58%. This means debris removal is incomplete, causing secondary discharges that worsen Ra and increase wire break risk. Compensate by: (1) increasing flush pressure to 8-10 bar, (2) reducing cutting speed by 20-40%, (3) using submerged cutting mode. Kunieda (2005) confirmed this empirically.

instruction: As a Mitsubishi/Sodick wire-EDM controller expert, explain the following dialect detail.
input: Agie Charmilles control-generation matrix — CNC 100 / CNC 123 / AgieVision / UNIQUA file formats differ
output: Agie Charmilles wire EDM machines under the GF Machining Solutions umbrella have 4 control generations with INCOMPATIBLE file formats. CNC 100 / CNC 123 / CNC 123D use .GEO (part geometry) + .JOB (job parameters) + .TEB / .TEC / .TED (machine technology / condition file). AgieVision (newer Agie ISO control) uses .ISO (G-code geometry) + .SBL (script / workpiece parameters + instructions) + .SBR (file list). UNIQUA is the modern (post-2015) HMI consolidating Agie + Charmilles UI patterns — runs ISO-based sequential or object-oriented programming. Critical gotcha for post-processor authors: 'Agie Charmilles' is a brand, NOT a single control — a Charmilles Robofil 510P ships with a different OS than an Agie CUT X with UNIQUA, even though both wear the GF badge; some configurations even ship with Fanuc controls. Always confirm machine + control + generator triplet before writing or porting a post. IPG (Intelligent Power Generator) is the modern generator family — 30% lower daily energy than the prior IPG generation. Robot macros use M920 / M921 (per Robofil manual rev 2004-06-23).

instruction: Advise on wire-EDM wire / consumable selection for the following.

instruction: As a wire-EDM CNC programming expert, explain the following programming practice.
input: UV taper programs: set all H-register offsets to zero
output: In JM Die's Mitsubishi FA-10S UV taper programs (E28xx family), ALL H-register wire compensation offsets are set to zero: H1=0.0+H175, H2=0.0+H175, etc. (and H175=0.0000 as well). This is confirmed in NOZE TEST.NC — a 5-pass UV taper stainless program where all 5 H-registers are 0.0000. The reason: taper wire compensation (kerf offset for an angled wire) cannot be decomposed into a simple 2D offset. The Mastercam Mitsubishi FA post processor handles the geometric taper compensation in the UV coordinates themselves, not via H-register offsets. Using non-zero H-registers in a taper program will double-compensate and produce an incorrect taper angle. Set H=0 for all taper jobs and let the post handle geometry.

instruction: As a wire-EDM CAM expert, explain the following.
input: Mastercam Wire lead-in/out arc geometry — Line+Arc in / Arc+Line out / 0.125" radius / 60° sweep / 0.3 max lead-out
output: Mastercam Wire Tutorial canonical lead motion: 'Line and arc for the lead in and Arc and line for the lead out. Starting and ending the toolpath with arc motion reduces the possibility of leaving a burr on the part.' Default geometric values: Arc radius 0.125, Arc sweep 60°, Maximum lead out distance 0.3 (shortens the lead out instead of traveling from cut-point back to start). These four numbers (radius / sweep / max-lead-out + the line+arc / arc+line pairing) are the canonical Mastercam Wire post defaults; deviating from them on JM Die E12xx-family jobs is what causes the 'burr at thread point' rejection the operator chases. Wizard rule: surface these defaults pre-filled in the lead-in/out form; flag any user override that picks tangent lead (straight line tangent to contour) instead of arc lead — straight tangent leaves the characteristic spike-burr at the part boundary because the discharge ramps up instantaneously instead of being eased on by the arc travel.

instruction: Explain the wire-EDM discharge physics behind the following.

instruction: Advise on wire-EDM speeds/feeds for the situation below.
input: Defense/ammo tooling: use E12xx heavy 5-pass with F0.06 rough feed for thread form integrity
output: JM Die's programs for defense and ammunition tooling (Choctaw Defense cannelure, Fiocchi .38-caliber dies, dated 2016) consistently use the E12xx heavy 5-pass family (E1281-E1285) with a very slow rough feed of F0.06 ipm (1.52 mm/min) — half the standard F0.12 rough feed. The 5 H-register offsets are: H1=0.00995, H2=0.00725, H3=0.00585, H4=0.00535, H5=0.0052 (all + H175). The slow rough pass is mandatory because the thread/cannelure profile has closely-spaced features (~0.033" pitch) where debris from one groove can short the discharge into the adjacent groove. At normal F0.12 rough speed, secondary discharge destroys thread root geometry. For any WEDM work with features spaced closer than 3× the wire diameter, reduce rough feed to F0.06 and increase to standard speed only after Pass 2 clears the initial recast.

instruction: Advise on wire-EDM machinability for the material/situation below.
input: Beryllium copper WEDM — 20% lower MRR than tool steel, brass wire + DI water standard, recast usually NOT removed
output: Beryllium copper (CuBe, typically C17200/C17500 — 1.8-2.0 wt% Be) is a high-strength, conductive, non-magnetic alloy used for injection-mold inserts (high thermal conductivity = fast cycle time), high-current connectors, and aerospace springs. WEDM machining-rate benchmark: ~20% lower than tool-steel MRR at the same generator settings. Standard setup: plain or zinc-coated brass wire 0.05-0.30 mm dia, deionized water dielectric, electrode-negative polarity (same as steel WEDM). The recast layer + heat-affected zone on CuBe is relatively SOFT vs the base alloy (opposite of Ti-6Al-4V) — and for most applications RECAST REMOVAL IS NOT NECESSARY because the soft outer layer wears off in service before it propagates a crack. When fatigue-critical (e.g. spring components), shot peening AFTER WEDM provides a smoother surface and improves fatigue life; abrasive or electrochemical polishing is the only path to fully remove recast + HAZ. SAFETY: beryllium dust is a respiratory hazard — WEDM is the SAFEST production method for CuBe parts (vs grinding) because all swarf stays bound in the dielectric. Filter the spent dielectric as hazardous waste — DO NOT regenerate the deionizer resin while Be is present.

instruction: Share the wire-EDM tactic for the following situation.
input: WEDM offset scheduling formula — offset_pass_N = wire_radius + spark_gap_pass_N + remaining_stock_pass_N
output: Canonical multi-pass offset-scheduling geometry from [[wedm-tactics-multipass-and-recast]] wiki: the H-register value programmed for pass N equals wire_radius + spark_gap_pass_N + remaining_stock_pass_N. (1) wire_radius — half the wire's physical diameter (0.125 mm for a 0.25 mm wire), constant across all passes. (2) spark_gap_pass_N — the over-burn / discharge-gap on this pass; decreases with each skim because discharge energy decreases (rough ~30 µm, skim 1 ~15 µm, skim 2 ~8 µm, skim 3 ~5 µm — material-and-thickness-dependent). (3) remaining_stock_pass_N — the workpiece material STILL to be removed after this pass + before the next; rough leaves the most stock for skim 1 to clean up; final skim leaves zero remaining stock. The strictly-decreasing JM Die offset cascade (0.0085→0.0064→0.0058→0.0053 inches for the E12xx 4-pass family) is this formula in action — each pass shrinks both the spark gap AND the remaining stock. Wizard / AI rule: when proposing offsets for an UNCALIBRATED job (material not in JM Die's tech tables), back-compute spark_gap_pass_N from per-pass discharge-energy table + look up wire_radius from chosen wire, and you can synthesize an offset cascade rather than guessing.

instruction: Advise on the wire-EDM machining practice below.
input: JM Die program optimization target — maximize productivity while maintaining Ra and tolerance
output: The ultimate goal of JM Die WEDM program optimization: maximize cutting area per hour (in²/hr) while achieving the specified Ra and tolerance. Optimization hierarchy: (1) Never sacrifice tolerance — ±0.0005" is sacred for die work. (2) Never exceed Ra spec — 16-20 µin standard, 12 µin for precision. (3) Maximize feed rate within physics limits for the material/thickness. (4) Minimize passes only if Ra spec allows — 3-pass for Ra 32+, 4-pass for Ra 16-20, 5-pass for Ra <16. (5) Use adaptive control (M90) to auto-optimize feed rate. The WEDMProgramOptimizerEngine computes expected improvements: typical gains are 10-25% cycle time reduction on amateur programs while matching or improving quality.

instruction: As a wire-EDM CNC programming expert, explain the following programming practice.
input: Makino DUO: G54/G55 WCS and radius list at program top
output: Makino DUO43/DUO64 programming best practice from Mastercam X8 post (Generic Makino 4X Wire TECH.pst): always use G54/G55 work coordinate offsets rather than G92 reference setting. Additionally, declare all wire radius offsets at the top of the program as a radius list (#2001 = 0.007, etc.) so all offsets are declared once and reused — this prevents register value conflicts when the same E-code condition is used on multiple chains. G92 output for Makino DUO has not been tested and is not recommended. Using G54/G55 also enables multi-setup programs (multiple cavities) without resetting the reference between contours.

instruction: As a wire-EDM CNC programming expert, explain the following programming practice.
input: Makino DUO: M17 compound code replaces separate thread/tank/flush sequence
output: On Makino DUO machines, M17 is a compound system code that simultaneously powers on, threads the wire, fills the tank, and activates flushing. It replaces the multi-step M06+M07 or Mitsubishi-style M78+M80+M82+M84 sequences. After cutting, M58 drains the tank. The Mastercam Makino post outputs M17 after each thread point automatically. Adding Mitsubishi-style M78/M80/M82/M84 blocks to a Makino program will cause a control alarm. Likewise, never use the Makino M17 on a Mitsubishi FA machine — it is not a Mitsubishi standard code.

instruction: Advise on the wire-EDM machining practice below.
input: SP43/SP64 carbide cutting: WC E-packs (5XXX series) start at Ra 51 µin — plan 4–5 passes to reach Ra 4 µin
output: When cutting tungsten carbide (WC or WC-Co) on the Makino SP43/SP64, the roughing E-pack Ra starts at 51 µin (1.3µm) — significantly lower than the 72 µin starting Ra for steel. This is because carbide ablates more slowly per discharge, producing a finer initial surface. The WC library (5025/5035/5045/5055/5065 rough + 52XX–52XX skims) achieves Ra 4 µin (0.10µm) in 4 passes for thicknesses up to 0.75", and 5 passes for 1.0"–1.25" sections. Offset values are slightly higher than steel at equivalent thickness due to the smaller spark gap on carbide (lower conductivity requires slightly larger compensation). Flushing note: use deionized water conductivity ≤ 5 µS/cm for carbide — higher conductivity causes electrolytic attack on the cobalt binder, creating subsurface micro-cracks invisible to surface inspection. Check conductivity every 4 hours when running long carbide programs.

instruction: Advise on the wire-EDM machining practice below.
input: SP43/SP64 copper (Cu) library: 3-pass High Precision achieves Ra 12 µin — use for electrode and fixture cutting
output: The Makino SP43/SP64 includes a dedicated Cu (copper) E-pack library (7XXX series: 7025/7035/7045/7055/7065 roughing + 72XX skims) for cutting copper electrodes for sinker EDM. Unlike the steel and carbide libraries which support 4–5 passes, the copper library completes in 3 passes, achieving Ra 12 µin (0.30µm) — sufficient for EDM electrode surface finish requirements. instruction: Advise on the wire-EDM machining practice below.
input: Tab/slug management for closed contour cuts
output: When cutting closed contours (die openings, through-holes), the slug will drop when the cut completes. For heavy slugs (>1kg): use 2-3 tabs (uncut bridges of 1-2mm width) to hold the slug, or apply adhesive (Super Glue or wax) before the final approach. For light slugs: program an M00 (optional stop) 5mm before the contour closes so the operator can support the slug. NEVER let slugs free-fall — they can jam the wire path or damage the lower guide.

instruction: Provide wire-EDM safety guidance for the following.
input: Safety: never reach into the tank during cutting
output: NEVER put hands into the dielectric tank while the machine is cutting. The voltage across the spark gap is 60-120V — not lethal for dry skin, but extremely dangerous with hands submerged in conductive water. Additionally, the wire moves at 10+ m/min and can lacerate skin instantly. Always pause the machine (feedhold, then M00) before reaching in. Keep the tank door interlocks functional — bypassing them is grounds for immediate termination in any reputable shop.
